title: Numerical Control Didn't De-skill Machinists — Average Skill Barely Moved
dek: Since the 1950s, people have feared that numerical control would de-skill machining trades. But Class A machinists and NC operators earned nearly the same hourly wage, and over three decades overall skill fell only about 1%.
why: Worth hearing for anyone tracking how automation rewrites skills and wages: this episode tests a widely believed claim against three data sets — training time, headcount and pay.
who: Investors watching automation and employment structure, and manufacturing engineers; also people building AI coding tools who want to know whether programmers will retrace the machinist's path.
skip: The hardware detail on early hard-wired NC and paper-tape control can be skipped.

points.h: A machinist's job isn't just cutting metal
points.body: A machinist doesn't just run a machine tool to cut metal. They work with designers to read two-dimensional drawings, reconstruct the three-dimensional part in their head, and spot in advance what can't be made, which is why geometry, trigonometry and algebra come into it. What's genuinely hard to replace is feel: the 1887 book The Complete Practical Machinist says lathe work is most demanding in feed and speed, the most varied, most complex and most deceptive part of the whole trade, requiring judgment, perception and alertness — the tool can sound and look fine while actually drifting off, even producing scrap or injuring someone. An experienced hand, using gauges plus feel, can detect dimensional changes as small as one half thousandths of an inch. Skill here equals judgment, and that is the bullseye of the later de-skilling debate.

points.h: Four years and eight thousand hours to make journeyman
points.body: In the first half of the twentieth century, machining was the single largest skilled manufacturing job for American men, and the standard entry path was a formal apprenticeship: generally four years, eight thousand hours; five years and ten thousand hours for tool and die makers. Someone who apprenticed at GE in the 1940s recalled spending the first half year learning basics in the shop, with classes three evenings a week in shop math, college physics, blueprint reading and electricity; then three and a half years rotating through various tools, starting at the drill press and switching about every six months. On finishing, the company certified you a journeyman, gave you a first set of tools or a cash bonus, and a raise — in his words, you were finally qualified for marriage. But it was never the only path: some became self-taught through pure shop experience and study at home, and there were courses claiming to teach you how to operate a machining shop, which you could call the 1930s coding bootcamp.

points.h: Riveting a boiler: nine machinists become one
points.body: Industrialization repeatedly does the same thing: pack the skill into the machine, then break the work into pieces. When Edison started making light bulbs in 1880, the factory was full of skilled craftsmen who understood glass and wire and knew from scratch how a bulb was made; as specialized machines built their skills in, the work was simplified and segmented, and a few all-round craftsmen were replaced by a large group of workers each knowing one operation. Riveting a boiler used to take nine skilled machinists; with a hydraulic riveter it became one skilled worker plus eight unskilled ones, the latter doing things like fixturing. In 1883 the young machinist John Morrison testified to Congress that the machining trade had been subdivided from the mid-1870s, and subdivided again after that, so that in sewing machine work, for instance, the jobs were split so finely that a person hardly counted as a machinist at all. NC is just one more step on that timeline.

points.h: Bosses hoping NC would save labor were disappointed first
points.body: NC controls the machine tool and the workpiece with pre-written instructions, with no need for a machinist to intervene directly by hand: a programmer translates the drawing into coordinates, punches them onto paper or plastic tape, and feeds it into the controller. It was invented in the 1950s, but at first served only the Air Force and aerospace, with specifications far beyond what ordinary shops and small job shops needed. Crucially, early NC was hard-wired, with limited functions, and a major change meant tearing the controller apart and rebuilding it — very inflexible. So shop owners hoping to lower worker skill with it were thoroughly disappointed: a mid-1960s survey by Lawrence Williams and Brian Williams found shops still needed operators with the same skills and technical knowledge, especially right after introduction; owners thought the risk of NC breaking down and causing expensive downtime was too high, and assigned their best employees to run the machine instead. Only once it matured did the advantage show — one NC drill press was estimated to equal three conventional machines.

points.h: Training shrank from five years to six months
points.body: In the 1970s computer technology accelerated NC's spread, and by 1980, 25% to 30% of machine tools sold in developed economies had NC. The real de-skilling evidence shows up in training time and headcount: a 1982 paper studying Swedish machining shops noted that NC operators needed at most 6 to 12 months of training, while lathe hands spent 4 to 5 years in the shop. In the cases the paper cited, one plant needed only 22 NC operators instead of 44 lathe hands; another replaced 63 qualified machine operators with 21 NC operators. In a developed country like Sweden, skilled workers willing to take night shifts were hard to find, and NC operators accepted stranger hours, so the machines didn't have to stop. As for whether that meant lower skill, nearly 80% of Canadian hand machinists surveyed in the 1980s agreed NC required fewer skills, while only half of those who had actually run NC saw it that way.

points.h: NC operators earned just twenty-one cents less an hour
points.body: Wages are a crude ruler for skill, but the result is counterintuitive. A 1989 study used 1981 US Bureau of Labor Statistics data to compare the average pay of 80,000 Class A machinists and NC operators in the machine tool industry: Class A machinists earned $9.72 an hour, NC operators $9.51. For comparison, Class A machinists still earned more than Class B and C machinists doing more repetitive work ($8.54 and $6.41); interestingly, there is evidence that some NC operators were recruited from Class B and C machinists, meaning they were actually on the receiving end of a raise. Of course wages are affected by region, unions and so on, and don't reflect job quality or the number of positions. Bill Bowman is the other side: as more people learned the skills he had, his CNC premium flattened, and a few years later, combined with layoffs, he was making only $20,000 a year.

points.h: Over thirty years overall skill fell only about 1%
points.body: Jeffrey Keefe's 1991 study examined three US Bureau of Labor Statistics surveys spanning 30 years and found overall skill levels fell by about 1% — essentially zero. That number directly knocks down the claim that numerical control de-skilled machinists. But the author also stressed that the unchanged average concealed changes in job composition: the work of skilled setup hands, semi-skilled machine operators and unskilled workers changed or disappeared, other tasks migrated to NC operators, and underneath it was very turbulent. So the more accurate statement is not that skill vanished but that its form changed — deep mastery of one thing was weakened and replaced by several other kinds of skill, such as understanding how the whole machine runs and reconstructing the logic of a failure, which is why operators say you can't just go tear into the fault, you have to work backward to how the accident happened.

points.h: AI coding is replaying this history
points.body: What the author sees is a parallel between AI coding and machining back then: early GitHub CoPilot and early Cursor only did simple completion or inserting a line, whereas AI coding systems have now evolved to be agentic — something modern CNC machine tools have not achieved. He specifically mentions a February 2026 case study by OpenAI's Ryan Lopopolo about an entirely new product built by a team of agents, with humans monitoring and steering. Programming, like machining back then, is one of America's dominant high-paying jobs; some things don't change — programmers still read code and judge where the problem is, only when it's time to fix it you tell the coding agent instead of opening a text editor, the same skills expressed differently. Some jobs will de-skill and decline, new fields may appear, and those are the NC operators of the AI coding era. What he remembers is Bill Bowman: you have to keep learning.

So perhaps those manual machinists are being a bit narrow-sighted in calling NC operators "less skilled". NC and CNC creating skill change doesn't mean operators became any less "skillful", if you get my driftwood.

One thoughtful 1991 study by Jeffrey Keefe studied three surveys done by the Bureau of Labor Statistics spanning 30 years and found that skill levels declined about 1% in aggregate. Essentially zero. But this unchanging average papers over the fact that the composition of the jobs certainly changed.

Early AI coding tools like GitHub CoPilot and early Cursor worked on simple autocomplete or line insertions. Then in recent days, AI coding systems have evolved to being "agentic" - a thing that modern CNC machines have yet to achieve.
For my part, the takeaway that most sticks with me are the experiences of the aforementioned Bill Bowman. You have to continually keep learning.
